definition: Architectural typology: classified by architectural form, spatial structure, and functional features to reveal cultural and historical context.
core_case: Demon caves can be classified by architectural form into natural karst caves, cliff tombs, waterside villas, and underground labyrinths — fantasy projections of pre-Ming architectural remains.

architecture_insights: The 5 major cave types cover the main Ming Dynasty architectural forms.
Natural karst caves are the most ancient, reflecting the Ming Dynasty's cave-worship tradition.
Cliff tombs derive from Han Dynasty burial customs, reflecting associations with the 'sacred heights'.
Waterside villas refract Jiangnan garden aesthetics; dragon palaces correspond to royal architecture.
Underground labyrinths correspond to imperial tombs, reflecting imaginings of the 'underworld'.
Mountain palaces fuse mountain worship with royal architecture and are the most luxurious.
Cave luxury correlates with demon background: grassroots demons live in karst caves, aristocrats in palaces.
